Section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) of 2008 prohibits, on or near the public road or in a building or vessel accessible to the public, participating in an unlawful gathering (samenscholing), defined in section 2.1(4) as 'a gathering of people who assume a threatening attitude, have malicious intentions or appear threatening', or, either as a member of a group or individually, imposing oneself unnecessarily, harassing others, fighting or otherwise disturbing public order (de orde verstoren).

Section 2.2(3) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV) of 2008 requires a person who is present on or near the public road at an event that attracts members of the public or at any occurrence that causes or is likely to cause disturbances (ongeregeldheden), or who is moving towards that event or occurrence, to immediately obey an order given by a police officer to move away in a given direction.

The applicants argue that the interference with their right to freedom of peaceful assembly was disproportionate.

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal held that the facts on 5 July 2011 led to a disturbance of public order on the entire Passeerdersgracht within the meaning of section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).

The Amsterdam Court of Appeal found it proven that the applicants had participated in an unlawful gathering or otherwise disturbed public order in breach of section 2.2(1) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).
The Amsterdam Court of Appeal found it proven that the applicants had failed to comply with a police order to disperse in breach of section 2.2(3) of the Amsterdam general municipal by-law (APV).

The Supreme Court noted that according to settled case-law of the Court, Article 11 of the Convention does not protect 'a demonstration where the organizers and participants have violent intentions', citing Schwabe and M.G. v. Germany, nos. 8080/08 and 8577/08, ECHR 2011 (extracts).
